source: Gong et al. (2026) To Think or Not To Think: large reasoning models in theory of mind tasks
finding: Nine models (o4-mini, o3, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3 8B/32B with and without reasoning, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3) on HiToM, ToMATO, ToMBench. Reasoning models do not reliably beat their non-reasoning twins; on ToMATO the non-reasoning twin wins in every pairing.
quote: reasoning models do not consistently outperform non-reasoning models and sometimes perform worse
limits: Multiple choice only; max 2048 output tokens may truncate long reasoning; Table 1 column alignment recovered from PDF text. No false-belief versus true-belief split, so it does not test the o1-preview 100/36 pattern.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 4: a stronger reasoning model is not a free ToM fix, so keep the scaffold's explicit perspective step and do not assume thinking mode replaces it.

source: Gong et al. (2026) reasoning effort and token-limit experiments
finding: More thinking hurts on hard higher-order items. o3 on HiToM falls as reasoning effort rises. Capping Qwen3 thinking tokens beats unlimited thinking. CoT on the non-reasoning model gets near o3 at far lower length.
numbers: o3 HiToM 0.838 at lowest effort to 0.693 at highest. Qwen3-8B-reasoning capped at 1,500 tokens 0.706 (above both modes). Qwen3-32B-reasoning capped at 1,000 tokens ToMATO 0.728 vs 0.714 uncapped. DeepSeek-V3 plus CoT HiToM 0.665 to 0.723; Qwen3-32B 0.525 to 0.647. Failed R1 answers cluster at 8,000-10,000 characters.
quote: extensive reasoning failure is triggered by the high cognitive load of complex tasks
limits: Effort effect weak on ToMATO and ToMBench. Best token cap differs by model and benchmark, so no single cap. Compute is partly matched here (CoT vs reasoning), the closest thing to gap 1 found.
agent_relevance: Supports a bounded, moderate reasoning budget per ToM step and a stop rule. Partly addresses gap 1 (compute-matched view) but not SimToM itself.

source: Gong et al. (2026) option-matching shortcut and Slow-to-Fast intervention
finding: Removing the multiple-choice options raises reasoning models on HiToM. Cutting off slow thinking when 'wait' repeats helps on hard items and does nothing on first-order items.
numbers: HiToM without options: DeepSeek-R1 0.549 to 0.691; Qwen3-8B-reasoning 0.481 to 0.629; non-reasoning Qwen3-8B 0.557 to 0.510. S2F: R1-Distill-Qwen-32B HiToM 0.571 to 0.701; negligible on ToMBench (first order).
limits: Open-source models only for S2F. Open-ended scoring on HiToM only because answers are extractive.
agent_relevance: Part of the ToM benchmark score is answer-list matching. Eval design for our agent should score free-form answers.

source: Bawatneh et al. (2026) OmniToM: benchmarking ToM via explicit belief modeling
finding: Asks models to write out every actor's belief propositions, not just answer a question. Models extract narrated facts better than actor-specific beliefs. Knowledge access (who knows what) is the weak dimension. Endpoint QA rank and belief-model rank differ.
numbers: 895 ToMBench stories, 22,343 labelled belief propositions. Best Stage 1 story-macro F1: Gemini-2.5 Pro 61.63. Stage 2 accuracy: Gemini-2.5 Flash 85.95%, Pro 85.54%. Knowledge Access accuracy 56.13-74.59% across models; Representation 54.33-89.01%. Order 1 beliefs lowest at 72.2%. Gemma-3 27B second on extraction (58.03 F1) but ninth on endpoint QA (53.95%). Judge change (GPT-5 to Llama-3.3) shifts F1 by 14.30-18.78 points.
limits: Reference beliefs written by Claude with human validation; absolute F1 depends on the judge. Stories from ToMBench; short, order up to 3. Only about 10 models.
agent_relevance: Bears on gap 3: a model-written ledger of who knows what is far from clean (F1 about 0.6), so a code-checked or cross-validated ledger is needed before gains stack. Supports scoring by the ledger, not only the final answer.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Learning Dynamic Belief Graphs for ToM reasoning, Table 2 (independent SimToM comparison)
finding: An unrelated lab ran SimToM as a baseline on SimpleToM, BigToM and OpenToM with 2025 open backbones. SimToM is not reliably better than plain LLM inference and is sometimes much worse on belief questions.
numbers: Belief accuracy SimToM vs plain LLM inference: BigToM Qwen3-32B 0.355 vs 0.900; Qwen3-8B 0.615 vs 0.830; Llama-3-70B 0.530 vs 0.812; DeepSeek-R1 0.740 vs 0.890. SimpleToM DeepSeek-R1 0.610 vs 0.860, but Llama-3-70B 0.980 vs 0.968 and Qwen3-32B 0.980 vs 0.947. Action accuracy SimToM higher on SimpleToM Qwen3-32B (0.950 vs 0.767), Llama-3-8B (0.900 vs 0.505), Qwen3-8B (0.780 vs 0.518). OpenToM mixed.
quote: SimToM uses a two-stage prompting framework
limits: Accuracies move in steps of 0.005, so about 200 items per cell. The paper's own method is the proposed one, so baselines may be less tuned. Different task framing from the SimToM paper (belief and action accuracy).
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 6: first independent SimToM numbers. Benefit is task dependent: helps action prediction in SimpleToM, hurts belief questions in BigToM. Do not rely on a perspective filter alone.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Dynamic Belief Graphs, Table 3 (first-person vs third-person prompting)
finding: Closest thing to a direct simulation test: same model, same items, only perspective changes. First-person framing (adopt the agent's view) recovers belief structure better than third-person, while CoT, few-shot and probabilistic prompting change little.
numbers: Wildfire evacuation data, six belief dimensions; the table's action accuracies match the Qwen3-8B row. Belief Spearman first vs third person: belief 2 .2952 vs .1046; belief 3 .1848 vs .1029; belief 5 .3824 vs .3241; belief 1 .4099 vs .4241 (third higher). Pairwise correlation .6643 vs .4071. Intermediate action accuracy .8443 vs .8439; final .9157 vs .8383. CoT pairwise .4036.
quote: first-person prompting consistently performs better in recovering belief structure
limits: Domain is human survey beliefs about wildfire risk, not false belief. Apparently one model. Mixed per-dimension results. Not a strict simulation vs theory test (no explicit rule-list arm).
agent_relevance: Partly addresses gap 5: perspective wording matters and CoT does not substitute. No theory-list arm, so gap 5 stays open.

finding: In a cooperative card game, first-order ToM (reading the partner's reason for a hint) tracks game score better than second-order ToM. Long-CoT reasoning models score far higher than plain LLMs.
numbers: Game score correlates with first-order ToM r=0.76 (p=0.00149) and second-order ToM r=0.58 (p=0.0301). Game scores: Llama-3.1-8B 3.47, GPT-4.1 7.20, Qwen3-8b 5.12, DeepSeek-R1 22.88, others 19-30, best 30.00 (SD 3.45). 30-50 five-player games per model; ToM scored 0-10 by an LLM judge.
quote: is a far stronger predictor of success than second-order ToM
limits: About 14 models, so correlations rest on 14 points; LLM-judge scoring; table score ranges are inconsistent with the stated max of 25.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly: in an interactive loop, reading the partner's rationale matters more than deep nesting. Keep first-order tracking cheap and reliable.

source: Riemer et al. (2025) Position: ToM benchmarks are broken for LLMs (functional ToM)
finding: Models predict a partner's next move about as well as a count table but fail to use that prediction to win. Literal ToM accuracy 92-97% with functional regret near the do-nothing level.
numbers: Rock-paper-scissors vs single-action partner: tabular RMax regret 0.083, ToM accuracy 97.4%; Llama-2 70B Chat regret 0.857 with ToM 92.1%; Llama-2 13B 1.015 with 96.7%; Mixtral 8x7B Instruct 0.542. Prompt variants on Mixtral: Social LM 0.643, CoT 0.648, QA 0.881. Oracle inputs (true actions and payoffs given) still worse than tabular. Social prompting did not close the gap. Random play regret is about 1.0.
quote: strong literal theory of mind performance does not necessarily imply strong functional theory of mind
limits: Mostly 2023-era open models (Llama-3 and Mistral Large 2 in appendix; the reasoning-model section was not read). Simple matrix games with simple partner policies.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the prediction-to-action gap persists in repeated play even with oracle inputs. Matches the SimpleToM judgment-behavior gap. Needs an explicit act-on-it step.

source: Cross et al. (2025) Hypothetical Minds ablations (ICLR 2025)
finding: An agent that keeps a list of hypotheses about the other agent and scores each by how well it predicts their next move beats ReAct, PlanReAct and Reflexion in embodied multi-agent tasks. Hypothesis scoring and refinement are the parts that matter.
numbers: Ablation on repeated rock-paper-scissors: modular prompting beat single-call prompting; adding hypothesis evaluation and refinement gave positive returns above 10 in all scenarios and the best result against a best-response bot. top_k=0 equals modular prompting; gains appear once any past hypothesis is kept; k above 3 gives diminishing returns, above 5 may hurt. Cost per 1000-step episode: PlanReAct $4, ReAct $6, a Reflexion row $10 and 45 min, HM-GPT3.5 $1; the HM-GPT4 row is garbled in extraction. GPT-4 beat GPT-3.5 and Llama-3-70B everywhere.
quote: the critical role of hypothesis evaluation and refinement within the ToM Module
limits: Authors' own system and environments; no token-matched comparison to best-of-N or CoT; HM uses 3 + k LLM calls per ToM step, so it spends more than PlanReAct. Cost table partly illegible.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 8: still one lab. A scored hypothesis list works in a game loop, but at higher cost, so gap 8 stays open on equal tokens.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Do ToM benchmarks need explicit human-like reasoning? (ToM-RL)
finding: Small models trained with RL or plain SFT reach benchmark scores above GPT-4o on Hi-ToM, sometimes with collapsed, very short reasoning. Benchmarks may be solvable by shortcuts.
numbers: Qwen 7B RL Hi-ToM 84.50% vs GPT-4o 69.00% and DeepSeek-v3 70.17%; GPT-4o-mini Hi-ToM 58.50%, ToMi 70.64%. 3B models: reasoning collapse with short answers and high accuracy. SFT often matches RL.
quote: current ToM benchmarks may be solvable without requiring the explicit, human-like simulation of mental states
limits: Trained on Hi-ToM-style synthetic data, so test items share structure with training. Small models only.
agent_relevance: A high score on template ToM sets does not show simulation or theory. Use held-out structure and process checks.

source: Zhu, Zhang, Wang (2024) Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others (re-read for steering table)
finding: Linear probes decode both the protagonist's and the oracle's (self) belief in Mistral-7B and DeepSeek-7B; the model's own view dominates. Steering along a direction that raises protagonist belief and lowers oracle belief (+TpFo) lifts false-belief accuracy on BigToM.
numbers: Baseline BigToM shows a large true-belief vs false-belief gap in both models. Steering row with TB/FB/Both: forward belief 0.99/0.98/0.97, forward action 0.98/0.81/0.79, backward belief 0.86/0.53/0.40 (the only row with these values; text says +TpFo remarkably improves). Probes above 75% accuracy in a subset of heads.
quote: possible to linearly decode the belief status from the perspectives of various agents
limits: Table 1 rows are interleaved in extracted text, so mapping of Mistral rows to steering modes is inferred (same limit as critique item 10). 7B models only; BigToM is GPT-written.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: steering effect is large but row mapping remains inferred. The result fits both theory and simulation readings.

source: Kulke, von Duhn, Schneider, Rakoczy (2018) Is implicit theory of mind a real and robust phenomenon? Systematic replication
finding: Preregistered large-scale replication of four anticipatory-looking implicit ToM tasks with original stimuli. Only one of four replicated; it failed once confounds were removed; no correlations between paradigms.
numbers: 1 of 4 paradigms replicated. Second set of studies: that one no longer replicated without confounds. Sample sizes not read (abstract via publisher metadata only).
quote: only one of the four paradigms was reliably replicated
limits: Abstract only (Crossref metadata); paper paywalled, WebFetch got 403. Concerns anticipatory looking, not violation-of-expectation looking time.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: strengthens K02. Never validate belief tracking with a single measure.

source: Rakoczy-lab preprint (2020) Small procedural differences matter: replication of Song, Onishi, Baillargeon and Fisher (2008)
finding: Violation-of-expectation (looking time) study of infants' false-belief updating after communication. Two studies failed a conceptual replication; a close direct replication reproduced the informative-statement effect but also found it with uninformative statements.
numbers: Studies 1a and 1b: failed conceptual replication. Study 2 (closer to original): effect for informative intervention, but the same effect for uninformative statements. Sample sizes not read.
quote: direct replication attempts for single studies need to follow the original design and procedure as closely as possible
limits: OSF abstract only. Concerns Song 2008, not Onishi and Baillargeon 2005 itself. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly: looking-time infant ToM is fragile and depends on procedure. No large-scale VoE replication of Onishi 2005 found; search budget ran out before ManyBabies 2 could be checked.

source: Preprint (2020) Infants differentiate successful and failed communication in a false-belief context
finding: 18-month-olds in a violation-of-expectation task expected an agent to search at the real location after full communication, at the old location with no communication, and showed no clear expectation after incomplete communication.
numbers: n=84 infants, three conditions (full, incomplete, no communication).
limits: OSF abstract only. Single lab; no replication reported in this record. Authors not verified.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a positive infant VoE result with moderate n, for contrast with failed anticipatory-looking replications. Replication status unknown.

source: Preprint (2026) Developmental unity of false belief understanding across cultures
finding: Preregistered cross-cultural study: change-of-location and aspectual false-belief tasks were robustly linked within children in rural Namibia and urban Germany, supporting a shared metarepresentational basis. Task format mattered for one group.
numbers: Hai||om N=65, Khwe N=35 (ages 3-9), Leipzig N=66 (ages 3-6). Format did not affect Leipzig or Khwe; Hai||om did better in the realistic format.
limits: OSF abstract only. Preprint. Does not separate simulation from theory.
agent_relevance: Background for K01: false-belief timing is partly format dependent, so use several item formats in our evals.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) Testing theory of mind in large language models and humans (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Battery of five ToM tests, GPT-4, GPT-3.5, LLaMA2-70B vs 1,907 humans. GPT-4 at or above humans on false belief, irony, hinting, strange stories; below on faux pas. GPT's faux-pas failure comes from hyperconservatism, not missing inference; LLaMA2's lead was a bias toward ascribing ignorance.
numbers: Human N=1,907 in total (about 50 per test: 50 irony, 51 faux pas, 48 hinting, 50 strange stories, 49 false belief). 15 LLM sessions per model. Irony GPT-4 above humans (P=0.040, r=0.32); faux pas GPT-4 below (P=5.42e-5, r=0.55); strange stories GPT-4 above (P=1.04e-5, r=0.60). False belief at ceiling, no inferential test. On perturbed false-belief items humans (N=757) also failed half.
quote: the poor performance of GPT originated from a hyperconservative approach towards committing to conclusions
limits: Per-item results of the N=757 perturbation study are in the supplement, not opened. The 757 sample is separate from the 1,907 battery sample.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open (no item table). Confirms response-bias reading: score ToM with controls that separate bias from inference.
